messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 39-year-old divorced construction worker, has been struggling with profound psychological distress following an incident where he witnessed his coworker being severely injured on the job. The traumatic event was particularly disturbing for Mark because it occurred during a routine day at work, a place where he had always felt secure and competent. Since then, his life has taken a drastic turn. Mark vividly recalls the day of the accident. He can still see the images of his coworker lying motionless on the ground, the metallic smell of blood mingling with the scent of concrete dust, and even taste the metallic tang in his mouth as he watched helplessly from a few feet away. These intense sensory memories are not just fleeting thoughts; they flood him whenever he is in environments that remind him of the construction site—like when he drives past similar sites or during his daily commute. What frightens Mark most is the sense that his beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed. He had always trusted in his own skills and the safety measures at work, but now he feels utterly helpless and inadequate, believing that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. This realization has driven him into a cycle of suppressing any anger or frustration he might feel about these events, as expressing those emotions only seems to confirm his feelings of inadequacy. To cope with the overwhelming memories, Mark often turns to gambling. He finds himself drawn to casinos and online betting sites where he can momentarily lose himself in excitement and distraction from his intrusive thoughts. This behavior is exacerbated when sensory triggers like the smell or taste associated with the event resurface, pushing him further into a cycle of avoidance. When the accident occurred, Mark tried to distance himself from the trauma by deliberately dissociating—leaving his body or blanking out whenever memories surfaced. However, this has only made the situation worse because it reinforces his belief that he cannot control what happens around him. The more he suppresses these feelings and engages in maladaptive behaviors like gambling, the stronger the negative appraisals become, leading to a tightening loop of distress. Mark’s occupation as a construction worker places him daily in environments where the triggers are ever-present. He avoids conversations about safety protocols at work because they remind him of his helplessness. This avoidance has strained his relationships with coworkers and supervisors, making it difficult for him to engage fully in his job. What finally brought Mark to seek help was an incident where he gambled away a significant portion of his savings, fearing that his financial instability would only confirm his feelings of inadequacy and reinforce the belief that he cannot prevent bad things from happening. He is most afraid that these patterns will continue to spiral out of control, destroying what little stability he has left. In therapy, Mark hopes to regain some sense of control over his life and to break free from the vicious cycle of negative thoughts and maladaptive behaviors. He longs for a way to process the traumatic event without it controlling every aspect of his daily existence.
